claims.claim: OpenStax's Principles of Management defines motivation as a force within or outside of the body that energizes, directs, and sustains human behavior; the word derives from the Latin movere, 'to move.'

Work motivation is the amount of effort a person exerts to achieve a certain level of job performance, and it has two components: direction (what a person wants to achieve) and intensity (how hard the person tries).

Extrinsic motivation is the drive to acquire something outside the person (external rewards such as pay and bonuses), while intrinsic motivation arises from performing the task itself because it is interesting or enjoyable; self-determination theory, as presented by OpenStax, ties intrinsic motivation to the needs for competence, autonomy, and relatedness.

Abraham Maslow proposed that human needs are arranged in a hierarchy (prepotency): physiological, safety and security, social, ego and esteem, and self-actualization; people act to satisfy unmet needs, and a satisfied need stops driving behavior.

OpenStax reports that research does not support the strict version of Maslow's hierarchy in which everyone moves through the five levels in a fixed order, though there is evidence that lower-order needs generally receive attention before higher-order ones.

Frederick Herzberg's motivator-hygiene theory holds that hygiene factors (job context: pay, working conditions, supervision, security) prevent dissatisfaction when adequate but do not create satisfaction or motivation, while motivators (job content: achievement, recognition, responsibility, growth) produce satisfaction and drive effort; satisfaction and dissatisfaction operate on different scales.

David McClelland's learned needs theory identifies three needs that vary across individuals: need for achievement (motivated to excel at difficult tasks, prefer moderate risk, seek feedback), need for affiliation (desire for warm relationships and teamwork), and need for power (desire to influence and control others).

McClelland distinguishes personal power seekers (controlling others for their own sake) from social power seekers (influencing others toward group goals); social power is the variant associated with effective managers.

Applied to work, the theories point to the same practical themes: fair pay and safe, decent conditions form the floor (they meet lower-order needs and prevent dissatisfaction), while meaningful work (challenging duties, responsibility) and recognition support esteem and growth needs that drive real effort.
Motivation is personal: needs differ in strength across individuals, no single theory describes everyone, and the theories are maps rather than fixed molds.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does everyone climb Maslow's hierarchy in the same fixed order?
positions: Popular version: people move through the five levels of needs in a strict sequence, and a lower level must be fully satisfied before the next activates.

Research review reported by OpenStax: the strict fixed-order version is not supported; people do not march through the five levels uniformly, though there is some evidence that lower-order needs are generally addressed before higher-order ones.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the five levels and the prepotency idea as Maslow proposed them, attributed to him, and then states the research caveat explicitly rather than presenting the pyramid as a proven law.

positions: Common assumption: higher pay directly produces stronger effort and loyalty.

Herzberg's position as presented by OpenStax: pay is a hygiene factor — adequate pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not create satisfaction or motivation; motivators such as achievement, recognition, and responsibility are the factors that drive lasting effort.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents Herzberg's classification attributed, and frames fair pay as the necessary floor beneath motivators rather than the engine of motivation.

Primary backbone for the lesson: Maslow's five-level hierarchy and prepotency plus the research caveat on fixed ordering; Herzberg's motivator-hygiene theory (hygienes as job-context dissatisfiers, motivators as job-content satisfiers); McClelland's learned needs (achievement, affiliation, power) and the two faces of power; intrinsic versus extrinsic motivation and self-determination theory (competence, autonomy, relatedness). sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 9.3: Maslow's Hierarchy of Needs
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture of the canonical OpenStax URL on 2026-08-22. Survey-level corroboration of Maslow's five need levels and the workplace application: physiological needs (food, shelter, clothing) motivate people to find work, and safety needs map to job security and protection from hazards. Used alongside 14.2 for the Maslow claims and the motivation-at-work framing; facts restated in original prose.

sourceRecords.title: Introduction to Business, Section 9.5: Herzberg's Motivator-Hygiene Theory
sourceRecords.notes: Read via Wayback Machine capture of the canonical OpenStax URL on 2026-08-22. Corroborates Herzberg's two-factor theory: motivators (satisfiers) are intrinsic job elements that lead to satisfaction, hygiene factors (dissatisfiers) are extrinsic elements of the work environment, and the opposite of satisfaction is not dissatisfaction. Also supports the claim that good working conditions keep employees but do not by themselves make them work harder. Facts restated in original prose.
